claims.text: Adding no more than 10 at% Pt or Pd to near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles modifies their local bonding and coordination environments.
Low Pt or Pd doping suppresses surface-atom diffusion at high temperature.
Low Pt or Pd doping suppresses chemical segregation at high temperature.
Low Pt or Pd doping preserves a single-phase solid-solution structure under catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions.
Noble-metal-induced changes in surface energy reduce phase separation and elemental clustering under thermal stress.
Pt or Pd doping lowers the mobility of non-noble species in the nanoparticles.
Pt or Pd doping reduces element-specific oxidation rates.
Pt or Pd doping reduces interdiffusion pathways that lead to segregation or phase transformation.
Relative to undoped nanoparticles, Pt- or Pd-doped nanoparticles will exhibit less grain growth during high-temperature exposure.
Relative to undoped nanoparticles, Pt- or Pd-doped nanoparticles will exhibit less surface roughening during high-temperature exposure.
Relative to undoped nanoparticles, Pt- or Pd-doped nanoparticles will show less phase separation and retain greater chemical homogeneity.
Undoped near-equiatomic nanoparticles will develop pronounced elemental segregation or secondary phases under the same service conditions.
The proposed stabilizing effect may degrade when noble-metal content exceeds approximately 10 at%.
Temperatures or reactive-species partial pressures far above design limits can cause macroscopic phase separation or surface restructuring.
The noble-metal concentration required for stability varies with alloy system, reaction environment, and thermal profile.
